utterance: Hello Samuel, I'm one of the doctors here. I can see you're uncomfortable. Can you tell me about the tummy pain — where it is, when it started, and what it feels like?
reply: Down here on the right side, low down. Started last night, about ten o'clock, so maybe fourteen hours. It is there all the time now, but at first it sort of came and went. Maybe a seven out of ten, though I am not one to complain.

awards.label: Whether the pain is constant or comes and goes

utterance: Did the pain start in that spot, or did it begin somewhere else and move there? Have you had any vomiting, fever, or change in your bowel habits?
reply: It started around my belly button and moved down to the right sometime overnight. I have felt sick since the early hours and threw up once this morning. I felt hot and a bit shivery last night. I went normally yesterday morning and have had nothing since, no diarrhoea.

awards.label: Red flag: Where the pain started and whether it has moved
Red flag: Fever, sweats or chills

utterance: Any pain when you pass urine, any blood in the urine, or discharge? And have you had anything like this before?
reply: No, weeing is normal, and I have never had anything like this.

awards.label: Whether he has had this pain before

utterance: Have you lost your appetite, and does the pain get worse when you move, cough, or walk? Any recent travel, unusual food, or anyone else unwell around you?
reply: I couldn't face breakfast and am not hungry at all, which isn't like me. Walking hurts, every bump in the car on the way here was awful, and coughing is the worst. I haven't been anywhere, just had the usual Mum's cooking on Sunday, and everyone at home and work is fine.

awards.label: Red flag: Whether moving, walking or coughing makes it worse
Anyone around him with vomiting or diarrhoea

utterance: Do you take any regular medicines, or have you taken anything for this pain? Any past operations or medical problems I should know about?
reply: I don't take any regular medicines, but I took a couple of paracetamol at six this morning and it didn't do much. I've never had an operation, I've still got my appendix as far as I know, and I don't have diabetes or any other medical problems.

finding: Flushed and uncomfortable. Lies very still on the couch and walks in slightly stooped.
Flat. No scars. Moves little with breathing.
Right lower quadrant: Marked tenderness, maximal at McBurney's point, with voluntary guarding. Central (periumbilical): Mild tenderness only. Elsewhere: soft and non-tender.
Right lower quadrant: Rebound tenderness present; he winces sharply. Elsewhere: no rebound tenderness.
Positive. Pressure in the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant.
Coughing causes sharp pain in the right lower quadrant; he holds his side.
Both testes normal lie, non-tender, no swelling.

result: Leucocytes trace, nitrites negative, blood trace, protein negative, ketones +.

utterance: A couple more things so I don't miss anything serious. Have you had pain in your shoulder, felt faint or dizzy, or had any chest pain or trouble breathing? Any blood in your stool?
reply: I haven't fainted or felt faint, I haven't noticed any chest pain or trouble breathing or pain in your shoulder, and there is no blood.

awards.label: Red flag excluded: Fainting or light-headedness

utterance:
Samuel, from what you've told me and from examining you, this looks like appendicitis. That's when a small pouch on the bowel, the appendix, gets inflamed and infected. The pain starting near the belly button and moving to the low right side, feeling sick, a mild fever, and the tenderness I found all fit with that.

This needs to be seen in hospital today, not treated at home as a stomach bug. The appendix can burst if it is left, which is more serious. I'm going to phone the emergency department so they expect you, and you should go straight there. Please don't eat or drink anything from now, in case you need an operation. Someone else should drive you — don't drive yourself.

I'll give you something stronger for the pain before you go. If the pain suddenly gets much worse, you start vomiting a lot, you feel faint, or you can't get to hospital quickly, call an ambulance on 000.
reply: An operation? Crikey, I was hoping I could just get some tablets and head back to the site. Are you sure I can't drive myself?

awards.label: Phone the emergency department with a handover

utterance:
I understand you want to get back to work, but this isn't something tablets will fix. If it is the appendix, it usually needs an operation to take it out, and waiting can let it burst, which is much more dangerous and a bigger operation.

Please don't drive yourself. You've had strong pain medicine that can make you drowsy, the pain is already bad, and you could become more unwell on the way. Get a lift, a taxi, or an ambulance if no one can take you. Go now, don't eat or drink, and tell them at the emergency desk that your GP has already called ahead about suspected appendicitis.

If you vomit repeatedly, the pain spreads across the whole tummy, you feel faint, or you can't get a lift within the next little while, call 000.
reply: Alright then, I will get someone to drive me.

awards.label: Can't-miss diagnosis considered: Perforated viscus with peritonitis
